item.title: Residential Cooling Load Design: A Sizing a Equipment Primer
item.description:
By the Editorial Team | Published: August 2026 | Last Updated: August 2026

The Sizing Decision That Quietly Shapes Every Cooling Project

Residential cooling load design is the discipline that decides how much cooling a house actually needs, what equipment can deliver it without overshooting, and how the ductwork will move that air without wasting capacity. It is a small stack of engineering steps, done in a specific order, and it happens before the first piece of equipment is priced. When it is skipped, the house gets a system that runs poorly for the next 12 to 15 years. When it is done, everything downstream, from indoor humidity to monthly utility bills, tends to fall into place.

This primer walks through the load-design workflow the way a residential HVAC engineer or a careful contractor works it: what the calculations are, what each one produces, and where the common failure points are hidden. It follows the three ACCA manuals that anchor the field, Manual J, Manual S, and Manual D, and treats climate as a first-class input rather than a footnote. The goal is not to teach anyone to run the calculations from scratch, but to make the outputs legible so the reader can tell a defensible design from a rule-of-thumb guess.

Why Cooling Load Design Is the First Real Decision

Most homeowners think of a cooling project as an equipment purchase. In practice, the equipment is a consequence of a set of numbers produced days or weeks earlier. Those numbers describe how much heat the house gains on a design-day afternoon, how much of that heat is sensible versus latent, and how quickly the load changes across the season.

Getting that number wrong by 20 percent is the difference between a system that dehumidifies properly and a system that short-cycles all summer. The Air Conditioning Contractors of America publishes the load-calculation procedure as Manual J, and the residential design version is currently in its eighth edition, commonly written as MJ8. It is the accepted standard for one and two-family dwellings across most North American code jurisdictions.

The Common Failure Modes

  • Sizing by square footage alone, using a rule of thumb like 500 or 600 square feet per ton.
  • Copying the tonnage of the outgoing system without asking whether that system was right to begin with.
  • Using generic climate inputs instead of the ACCA-approved 1 percent and 99 percent design temperatures for the specific location.
  • Ignoring latent load in humid climates, where moisture removal often drives the sizing more than raw cooling capacity.

Each of these shortcuts routinely produces oversized equipment. Oversized cooling equipment satisfies the thermostat quickly and shuts off before removing enough moisture, which leaves the house cool and clammy. That is the humidity complaint homeowners describe as the air feels sticky even though the AC is running.

What Manual J Actually Calculates

Manual J produces two numbers per house: the total sensible cooling load and the total latent cooling load, both expressed in Btu per hour at design conditions. Sensible load is the heat the system must remove to lower the air temperature. Latent load is the moisture the system must remove to lower the humidity. Together they define the required equipment capacity.

A room-by-room Manual J also produces per-room loads, which are the inputs Manual D needs to size individual ducts and diffusers. Building only a whole-house block load skips the room-level detail and forces the duct designer to guess. The room-by-room version is the one the ACCA design-verified process expects.

Because the outputs directly determine whether the equipment matches the house, the calculation itself deserves scrutiny. For a deeper look at how load calculation errors show up in one of the harder North American markets, this companion analysis on why Manual J load calculations matter for accurate residential cooling sizing walks through the specific ways the numbers get distorted in hot-humid conditions.

Inputs the Calculation Actually Needs

A Manual J load is only as trustworthy as the inputs the operator enters. The core inputs the software will not accept default values for are:

  • Building envelope details, including wall assemblies, insulation R-values, and window U-values with solar heat gain coefficients.
  • Infiltration rate, measured by blower-door test or estimated in air changes per hour at 50 pascals.
  • Design temperatures for the specific location, taken from ACCA climatic tables.
  • Internal gains from occupants, lighting, and appliances at the design hour.
  • Duct system location (conditioned versus unconditioned space) and measured or estimated leakage rate.

Any of these entered wrong will move the total load by hundreds of Btu per hour, and in aggregate the input errors compound rather than cancel.

From Load to Equipment: Manual S in Plain Terms

Manual J tells the designer how much cooling the house needs. Manual S is how the designer picks equipment that can actually deliver that cooling under the local design conditions. It is a matching exercise between the load calculation and the manufacturer expanded performance data, and it enforces limits on how far the selected equipment can exceed the load.

The ACCA cap for a straight-cool system is that total sensible capacity at design conditions must not exceed 115 percent of the sensible load. For heat pumps in cooling mode the cap is 125 percent. These caps exist because equipment above them will short-cycle on cool days and remove less moisture than a properly matched unit. Manufacturers publish sensible and latent capacity separately across a grid of outdoor and indoor conditions; Manual S is the process of reading those grids honestly rather than picking the nameplate tonnage nearest to the load.

The Duct Half of the Equation: Manual D

Even a correctly selected system fails if the duct system cannot deliver its capacity to the right rooms at the right static pressure. Manual D is the duct-design procedure that takes the per-room loads from Manual J, converts them to airflow requirements, and sizes trunks, branches, and diffusers to move that air within the equipment rated external static pressure.

A duct system built without Manual D is the reason so many technically correct equipment selections still produce hot rooms and cold rooms in the same house. The airflow arrives unevenly, the return path is undersized, and the blower ends up fighting static pressure it was never rated for.

Hot-Humid Climates Change the Math

Cooling design in climate zones with high latent loads is a different exercise from cooling design in a dry climate. In hot-humid conditions, latent load frequently reaches 25 to 40 percent of the total cooling load, which means moisture removal, not temperature reduction, is often the binding constraint on equipment selection.

In those climates, oversizing has a double penalty: the system reaches temperature setpoint too quickly, shuts off, and never runs long enough to pull the moisture out of the air. The right-sized system runs longer at a lower capacity fraction and holds indoor relative humidity in the 45 to 55 percent comfort band. IECC Climate Zones 1A, 2A, and 3A cover the U.S. Gulf Coast, the Southeast, and southern Texas, and are the regions where the cost of getting sizing wrong is highest.

The Three ACCA Manuals at a Glance

Manual What it produces Where it fits Common failure if skipped
Manual J (MJ8) Sensible and latent cooling loads, room by room, in Btu/hr Step 1 of design Oversized equipment sized to a rule of thumb
Manual S Specific equipment model selected from the load, capped at 115 percent cooling or 125 percent heat pump Step 2 of design Nameplate-tonnage picking without checking expanded performance data
Manual D Duct sizes, layouts, and diffuser selection to hit per-room airflow at target static pressure Step 3 of design Rooms that never reach setpoint, blower over-static

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a rule-of-thumb sizing ever acceptable?

Rule-of-thumb sizing is not acceptable for a residential cooling installation that is expected to control humidity, deliver even room temperatures, and last a normal service life. It gets used because it is fast, not because it produces good outcomes. Rules like 500 or 600 square feet per ton were developed for houses with poor envelopes and leaky ducts, and they systematically oversize modern homes with better insulation and tighter shells. The 2024 International Residential Code and most state adoptions reference ACCA Manual J as the required calculation for equipment sizing.

How long does a proper Manual J calculation take?

A complete room-by-room Manual J for a typical single-family house takes a competent operator three to six hours from a good set of plans, or six to ten hours if the operator has to measure the house first. Software such as Wrightsoft Right-J or Elite Software Rhvac handles the math, but the input work, entering wall assemblies, window specifications, infiltration values, and duct locations, is the time-consuming step. A shorter turnaround usually means the operator used generic assumptions instead of the actual building.

What is the difference between a block load and a room-by-room load?

A block load produces one total for the whole house. A room-by-room load produces a separate total for each conditioned space. The block load can size the outdoor unit, but it cannot support duct design because it does not tell the duct designer how much air each room needs. ACCA Quality Installation standard and most third-party design-verification programs require the room-by-room version.

Why does Manual S cap sensible capacity at 115 percent of the load?

The 115 percent cap keeps equipment from being so oversized that it satisfies the thermostat before it has run long enough to remove moisture. A system sized at, say, 140 percent of the sensible load will cycle on and off in short bursts on mild days, leaving indoor relative humidity above the comfort band. The cap is a design constraint, not a suggestion; the ACCA-approved software will flag selections that exceed it.

How much does latent load matter compared to sensible load?

Latent load is the amount of cooling capacity a system spends removing moisture rather than lowering air temperature. In dry climates, latent load might be 10 percent of total load and can be treated as a secondary concern. In hot-humid climates such as U.S. IECC Zones 1A and 2A, latent load routinely runs 25 to 40 percent of total load, which changes both equipment selection and the operational profile. In those climates, a designer will usually favor variable-capacity equipment that can run long low-capacity cycles instead of short high-capacity ones.

Do the same rules apply to heat pumps as to straight-cool systems?

The load calculation is the same, but Manual S applies a slightly looser oversizing cap for heat pumps in cooling mode (125 percent versus 115 percent for cooling-only). The extra allowance exists because heat pumps also have to satisfy heating loads, and a small oversize helps heating capacity in the shoulder seasons without seriously compromising dehumidification. Variable-speed and inverter-driven heat pumps handle the tension better than single-stage units because they can modulate down to match part-load conditions.

What is the design temperature and where does it come from?

The cooling design temperature is the outdoor dry-bulb temperature that a location exceeds only 1 percent of the hours in a typical cooling season, paired with a coincident wet-bulb temperature for moisture. ACCA publishes these values in Manual J design condition tables and updates them from ASHRAE climatic design data. Using a design temperature that is too high inflates the load; using one that is too low undersizes for the actual worst days. The ACCA-listed value for the location is the defensible input.

Can the same load calculation be reused for the next equipment change 15 years later?

Only if the building envelope has not changed. New windows, added attic insulation, sealed ducts, a finished basement, or a room addition all shift the load, and the shifts can be large. A house that received major envelope upgrades will usually need a smaller cooling system than the original design called for. The correct workflow is to rerun the Manual J whenever equipment is replaced, using the current state of the envelope rather than the original design assumptions.

item.title: Manual S Equipment Selection After the Load Calculation
item.description:
By the Editorial Team | Published: August 2026 | Last Updated: August 2026

The Step Between the Load Calculation and the Equipment Order

Manual S is the ACCA procedure for selecting a specific piece of equipment once the load is known. It sits between Manual J, which produces the load, and Manual D, which sizes the duct system. Skipping it is the single most common way a properly calculated load still ends up matched to the wrong equipment. The step is short, the math is not difficult, and the outputs are directly tied to whether the installed system will actually control temperature and humidity at design conditions.

The exercise is a matching one. The load calculation gives a sensible cooling requirement and a latent cooling requirement, both in Btu per hour at the local design conditions. The manufacturer publishes performance data for each condensing unit and indoor coil combination across a grid of outdoor and indoor temperatures. Manual S is the process of reading that grid at the design conditions for the location, then checking that the selected equipment sits within the ACCA-permitted oversizing window.

What Expanded Performance Data Actually Shows

Nameplate tonnage is a marketing number. Real equipment capacity varies with outdoor temperature, indoor return-air temperature, indoor return-air wet-bulb, and indoor airflow. Manufacturers publish this in expanded performance tables, sometimes called AHRI-certified or ARI performance data, and every ACCA-approved Manual S calculation reads from these tables at the design conditions rather than the AHRI rating point.

The AHRI rating point is 95 degrees Fahrenheit outdoor dry-bulb, 80 degrees Fahrenheit indoor dry-bulb, and 67 degrees Fahrenheit indoor wet-bulb, at a specified airflow. Real design days rarely match those exact conditions, and the actual delivered capacity will move up or down accordingly.

The values a Manual S calculation extracts from the table:

  • Total cooling capacity at the local design outdoor and indoor conditions.
  • Sensible cooling capacity at those same conditions, which is what actually cools the air.
  • Latent cooling capacity, calculated as total minus sensible, which is what removes moisture.
  • The airflow the coil requires to deliver those capacities.

The Oversizing Caps and Why They Exist

ACCA Manual S sets hard upper bounds on how far the selected equipment can exceed the calculated sensible load. For a straight-cool system, sensible capacity at design cannot exceed 115 percent of the sensible load. For a heat pump operating in cooling mode, the cap is 125 percent. The extra headroom for heat pumps recognizes that the same equipment has to satisfy heating loads too, and a small oversize helps at low ambient temperatures.

Above the cap, the system runs shorter and shorter cycles on typical days. Short cycles reduce runtime, and reduced runtime reduces the number of hours the coil is actively pulling moisture out of the air. In cooling-dominant climates the practical outcome is a house that is at temperature setpoint but reading 60 or 65 percent relative humidity, which occupants describe as clammy or muggy even though the thermostat reads 74 degrees.

The most common symptoms of a Manual S cap violation, in the order occupants notice them:

  • Indoor humidity readings above 55 percent during the cooling season, even at temperature setpoint.
  • Very short run cycles (under 10 minutes) on mild summer days.
  • Uneven room temperatures, because short cycles do not last long enough to distribute air through the duct system.
  • Higher-than-expected utility bills, driven by the compressor high current draw at startup relative to its short runtime.

Sensible Heat Ratio and Why It Matters

Sensible heat ratio, or SHR, is the fraction of a system total cooling capacity that goes to lowering air temperature rather than removing moisture. A high-SHR unit (0.80 or higher) is efficient at temperature reduction but weak at moisture removal. A low-SHR unit (below 0.75) is better suited to humid climates where the calculated latent load is a large fraction of the total.

Manual S requires the selected equipment SHR at design conditions to match the house calculated load SHR within an acceptable tolerance. A house with a 0.72 load SHR paired with a 0.82 SHR unit is a design mismatch even when the total capacity looks correct, because the unit will remove too little moisture.

Single-Stage, Two-Stage, and Variable-Speed Selection

The equipment class affects how the Manual S check plays out. Single-stage units either run at full capacity or off; they hit the sensible cap the fastest and are the hardest to size for humid climates. Two-stage units run at a reduced capacity most of the time and step up to full on hot afternoons, which softens the cycling penalty. Variable-speed or inverter-driven units modulate continuously between roughly 25 percent and 100 percent of nameplate capacity, which lets a designer size closer to the load without oversizing risk.

Equipment class Turndown range Manual S oversizing tolerance Best fit
Single-stage None (100 percent only) Tight; keep near 100 percent of load Dry climates, small budget projects
Two-stage ~65 percent low / 100 percent high Slightly wider Mixed climates, most retrofits
Variable-speed / inverter ~25 percent to 100 percent Widest; long low-capacity runs Hot-humid climates, high-performance homes

Is Manual S required by code or is it optional?

Manual S is referenced by the International Residential Code alongside Manual J and Manual D as the accepted procedure for equipment selection. Most state code adoptions incorporate the IRC references, which makes Manual S part of the required design workflow rather than an optional add-on. Enforcement varies by jurisdiction. The design-verification programs run by third parties, including the Energy Star Certified Homes and the ACCA Quality Installation standards, explicitly require documented Manual S selection.

Can nameplate tonnage be used instead of expanded performance data?

Nameplate tonnage is unsuitable for Manual S because it is measured at the AHRI rating point (95 degrees outdoor, 80 degrees indoor, 67 degrees wet-bulb) which almost never matches a specific location design conditions. A three-ton nameplate unit delivers less than 36,000 Btu/hr on a 100-degree afternoon and more on a 90-degree afternoon. Reading the manufacturer expanded performance table at the actual design conditions is the only way to know delivered capacity.

What happens when the selected equipment exceeds the 115 percent cap?

Selections above the 115 percent sensible cap trigger a flag in ACCA-approved Manual S software (Wrightsoft Right-Suite, Elite Rhvac, and Cool Calc all enforce it). Designers who accept the flag usually accept a documented dehumidification problem. In practice, occupants notice the humidity within the first cooling season, and the fix is either equipment replacement or the addition of a whole-house dehumidifier, either of which costs more than picking correctly the first time.

How does variable-speed equipment change the Manual S check?

Variable-speed equipment can modulate down to roughly 25 percent of nameplate capacity, which means short-cycling risk is dramatically lower even at the upper end of the oversizing window. A designer can select closer to the load without triggering the same humidity penalty a single-stage unit would produce. The Manual S check is still required and the caps still apply, but the practical consequence of sitting near the cap is much smaller for a modulating unit than for a single-stage unit.

Does Manual S apply to ductless mini-split systems?

Manual S applies to mini-splits, and the manufacturer expanded performance data is still the correct input. The additional consideration for ductless is that a multi-zone system connected indoor unit capacity often exceeds the outdoor unit simultaneous capacity, and the Manual S selection has to account for the diversity factor the manufacturer publishes. Skipping this step routinely produces mini-split installations that satisfy no zone properly at design conditions.

Where does the coil airflow fit into the selection?

Coil airflow is one of the axes on the expanded performance table, and every published capacity assumes a specific airflow across the coil. If the duct system cannot deliver that airflow, the actual sensible capacity drops and the latent capacity rises, which shifts the sensible heat ratio. Manual S selection includes verifying that the airflow the coil needs is what the duct system will actually provide, which loops the calculation back to Manual D.

How often does the selected model differ from what the contractor would have chosen by rule of thumb?

In the majority of retrofits, a proper Manual J and Manual S produces a smaller system than the outgoing unit, often by half a ton to a full ton. The rule of thumb almost always oversizes because it assumes the pre-modern envelope conditions the original industry rules were built around. On new construction the difference is smaller but usually still points to a smaller unit than the builder default.

Does the Manual S output name a specific model number?

The output names a specific outdoor unit and indoor coil combination, because performance data is only valid for matched combinations. Mixing an outdoor condenser with a coil it was not tested against invalidates the manufacturer performance table and voids the Manual S selection. The AHRI directory publishes the certified matched combinations and their expanded performance data.

ACCA Manual S sets hard upper bounds on how far the selected equipment can exceed the calculated sensible load. For a straight-cool system, sensible capacity at design cannot exceed 115 percent of the sensible load. For a heat pump operating in cooling mode, the cap is 125 percent. The extra headroom for heat pumps recognizes that the same equipment has to satisfy heating loads too, and a small oversize helps at low ambient temperatures.

Above the cap, the system runs shorter and shorter cycles on typical days. Short cycles reduce runtime, and reduced runtime reduces the number of hours the coil is actively pulling moisture out of the air. In cooling-dominant climates the practical outcome is a house that is at temperature setpoint but reading 60 or 65 percent relative humidity, which occupants describe as clammy or muggy even though the thermostat reads 74 degrees.

The most common symptoms of a Manual S cap violation, in the order occupants notice them:

  • Indoor humidity readings above 55 percent during the cooling season, even at temperature setpoint.
  • Very short run cycles (under 10 minutes) on mild summer days.
  • Uneven room temperatures, because short cycles do not last long enough to distribute air through the duct system.
  • Higher-than-expected utility bills, driven by the compressor high current draw at startup relative to its short runtime.

Sensible Heat Ratio and Why It Matters

Sensible heat ratio, or SHR, is the fraction of a system total cooling capacity that goes to lowering air temperature rather than removing moisture. A high-SHR unit (0.80 or higher) is efficient at temperature reduction but weak at moisture removal. A low-SHR unit (below 0.75) is better suited to humid climates where the calculated latent load is a large fraction of the total.

Manual S requires the selected equipment SHR at design conditions to match the house calculated load SHR within an acceptable tolerance. A house with a 0.72 load SHR paired with a 0.82 SHR unit is a design mismatch even when the total capacity looks correct, because the unit will remove too little moisture.

Single-Stage, Two-Stage, and Variable-Speed Selection

The equipment class affects how the Manual S check plays out. Single-stage units either run at full capacity or off; they hit the sensible cap the fastest and are the hardest to size for humid climates. Two-stage units run at a reduced capacity most of the time and step up to full on hot afternoons, which softens the cycling penalty. Variable-speed or inverter-driven units modulate continuously between roughly 25 percent and 100 percent of nameplate capacity, which lets a designer size closer to the load without oversizing risk.

Equipment class Turndown range Manual S oversizing tolerance Best fit
Single-stage None (100 percent only) Tight; keep near 100 percent of load Dry climates, small budget projects
Two-stage ~65 percent low / 100 percent high Slightly wider Mixed climates, most retrofits

Is Manual S required by code or is it optional?

Manual S is referenced by the International Residential Code alongside Manual J and Manual D as the accepted procedure for equipment selection. A three-ton nameplate unit delivers less than 36,000 Btu/hr on a 100-degree afternoon and more on a 90-degree afternoon. Reading the manufacturer expanded performance table at the actual design conditions is the only way to know delivered capacity.

In practice, occupants notice the humidity within the first cooling season, and the fix is either equipment replacement or the addition of a whole-house dehumidifier, either of which costs more than picking correctly the first time.

Variable-speed equipment can modulate down to roughly 25 percent of nameplate capacity, which means short-cycling risk is dramatically lower even at the upper end of the oversizing window. A designer can select closer to the load without triggering the same humidity penalty a single-stage unit would produce. The Manual S check is still required and the caps still apply, but the practical consequence of sitting near the cap is much smaller for a modulating unit than for a single-stage unit.

Manual S applies to mini-splits, and the manufacturer expanded performance data is still the correct input. The additional consideration for ductless is that a multi-zone system connected indoor unit capacity often exceeds the outdoor unit simultaneous capacity, and the Manual S selection has to account for the diversity factor the manufacturer publishes. Skipping this step routinely produces mini-split installations that satisfy no zone properly at design conditions.

Where does the coil airflow fit into the selection?

Coil airflow is one of the axes on the expanded performance table, and every published capacity assumes a specific airflow across the coil. If the duct system cannot deliver that airflow, the actual sensible capacity drops and the latent capacity rises, which shifts the sensible heat ratio. Manual S selection includes verifying that the airflow the coil needs is what the duct system will actually provide, which loops the calculation back to Manual D.

How often does the selected model differ from what the contractor would have chosen by rule of thumb?

In the majority of retrofits, a proper Manual J and Manual S produces a smaller system than the outgoing unit, often by half a ton to a full ton. The rule of thumb almost always oversizes because it assumes the pre-modern envelope conditions the original industry rules were built around. On new construction the difference is smaller but usually still points to a smaller unit than the builder default.

Does the Manual S output name a specific model number?

The output names a specific outdoor unit and indoor coil combination, because performance data is only valid for matched combinations. Mixing an outdoor condenser with a coil it was not tested against invalidates the manufacturer performance table and voids the Manual S selection. The AHRI directory publishes the certified matched combinations and their expanded performance data.

item.description:
By the Editorial Team | Published: August 2026 | Last Updated: August 2026

Why Hot-Humid Climate Zones Break Cooling Design Assumptions

IECC Climate Zone 2A covers the Gulf Coast band of the United States: the lower half of Texas, most of Louisiana and Mississippi, southern Alabama, most of Florida, and coastal Georgia. It is the zone where residential cooling design assumptions built for dry or mixed climates start to fail visibly, because moisture is the binding constraint on comfort for most of the cooling season. A load calculation and equipment selection that would work fine in Zone 4A can produce a humidity-complaint installation in Zone 2A even when the math is technically correct.

The distinguishing feature of Zone 2A is not the peak temperature. Peak dry-bulb design temperatures in the zone typically sit between 92 and 98 degrees Fahrenheit, which is not extreme by U.S. standards. The distinguishing feature is the coincident wet-bulb temperature, which routinely runs 76 to 80 degrees during design conditions and pushes latent load to 30 percent or more of the total cooling load. That shifts almost every design decision.

What Changes in the Manual J Calculation

A Manual J run for a Zone 2A house uses the ACCA-listed 1 percent design dry-bulb and coincident wet-bulb for the specific city, not a rounded regional value. Representative city design conditions:

  • Houston, TX: 96F dry-bulb / 77F wet-bulb
  • Mobile, AL: 94F dry-bulb / 78F wet-bulb
  • New Orleans, LA: 93F dry-bulb / 78F wet-bulb
  • Orlando, FL: 93F dry-bulb / 77F wet-bulb
  • Miami, FL: 91F dry-bulb / 79F wet-bulb

Each of those pairs produces different sensible and latent split ratios, and equipment selection follows accordingly.

Infiltration is a bigger factor in Zone 2A than in cooler climates, because outdoor air brought in through leaks carries moisture that has to be removed indoors. A house with 5 air changes per hour at 50 pascals in a hot-humid climate imports a measurable latent load that the equipment has to overcome before it can start satisfying the sensible load. Blower-door testing to establish the actual infiltration rate, rather than defaulting to a table value, is one of the highest-leverage inputs to the calculation in this zone.

Equipment Selection Choices That Look Different Here

The equipment choices that work in a dry climate stop working in Zone 2A once latent load crosses roughly 25 percent of total load. Single-stage equipment sized to the sensible load leaves latent capacity uncovered. Oversized equipment satisfies the thermostat and shuts off before pulling humidity down. Variable-capacity equipment is the class most designers reach for first in this zone, because it can run long low-capacity cycles that keep the coil cold and moisture removal continuous.

The design considerations that shift most sharply in Zone 2A:

  • Sensible heat ratio (SHR) of the selected equipment should sit at or below 0.75 to match the house typical load SHR.
  • Airflow across the coil is often reduced below the 400 CFM per ton default (to roughly 350 CFM per ton) to increase moisture removal.
  • Whole-house dehumidifiers are frequently added as a second-stage moisture control for shoulder-season conditions when the AC does not run enough.
  • Duct systems in unconditioned attics carry a large penalty, because Zone 2A attics regularly hit 130 degrees and drive both conduction loss and latent gain from duct leakage.

The Attic-Duct Penalty

Ductwork located in an unconditioned attic is standard in Zone 2A construction and is one of the largest sources of hidden capacity loss. Even a well-sealed duct system loses meaningful capacity to attic temperatures, and a duct system with the code-typical 6 percent leakage rate loses substantially more. Bringing the ducts into conditioned space, or building an unvented sealed attic, is the design move that produces the largest single reduction in cooling load for many Zone 2A retrofits.

The Comfort Metric That Matters Most

In dry climates, the primary comfort metric is dry-bulb temperature at the thermostat. In Zone 2A, indoor relative humidity is the comfort metric that shows up first in occupant complaints. A house at 74 degrees and 45 percent RH feels comfortable; the same house at 74 degrees and 62 percent RH feels uncomfortable, and residents will lower the thermostat to compensate, which increases energy use without solving the underlying moisture problem.

Indoor condition Occupant experience Design implication
74F / 45 percent RH Comfortable, no moisture complaint Target for correctly sized system
74F / 55 percent RH Comfort edge; noticeable in cool rooms Acceptable ceiling per ACCA guidance
74F / 62 percent RH Clammy; mold risk in wall assemblies System is oversized or has SHR mismatch
74F / 70 percent RH Actively uncomfortable; visible condensation Design failure; add dehumidification or resize

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Climate Zone 2A treated differently than warmer Zone 1A?

Zone 1A (roughly southern Florida) has slightly higher latent loads and lower diurnal temperature swing, but the design approach is broadly the same as Zone 2A. Zone 2A is the larger and more diverse zone, spanning Houston, New Orleans, Mobile, Orlando, and Charleston, and it captures most of the U.S. hot-humid construction market. The design principles that apply in 2A also apply in 1A with minor tightening on latent-capacity margins.

Does a high-SEER system automatically handle humidity better?

SEER measures energy efficiency, not dehumidification performance. A high-SEER single-stage unit can be a poor dehumidifier because the efficiency comes from a large evaporator that produces a high sensible heat ratio. Two-stage and variable-speed units at similar SEER ratings usually handle humidity better because their run pattern favors long low-capacity cycles. The SEER number alone does not predict humidity outcomes in Zone 2A.

What indoor humidity range should a Zone 2A design target?

The industry-accepted range for occupant comfort and building durability is 45 to 55 percent relative humidity indoors during the cooling season. Below 45 percent is unusual to hit in this zone without active dehumidification and is not necessary for comfort. Above 55 percent starts to be noticeable, and above 60 percent creates conditions for mold growth in wall assemblies and behind furniture on exterior walls. ASHRAE Standard 55 uses this range as its thermal comfort envelope.

When is a supplemental dehumidifier the right call?

Supplemental dehumidifiers become a design choice when the house has shoulder-season conditions (spring and fall) where outdoor temperature is mild but outdoor dew point is high. In those weeks the AC does not run enough to control humidity, and indoor RH drifts up regardless of how well the AC is sized. Whole-house ducted dehumidifiers in the 90-to-130 pint per day range address this gap without oversizing the primary cooling equipment.

How much does bringing ducts into conditioned space actually save?

Moving ducts from an unconditioned vented attic into conditioned space typically reduces measured cooling energy use by 10 to 20 percent in Zone 2A homes, according to Building America research from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. The design-load reduction from the change is often enough to justify a smaller nominal tonnage on equipment replacement, which lowers first cost and improves humidity control simultaneously.

Does building tightness make the humidity problem worse?

Building tightness reduces the moisture load imported by infiltration, which makes the humidity problem easier to control, not worse. The misconception that tight houses have moisture problems usually traces to tight houses without properly designed ventilation, where indoor moisture generated by occupants accumulates. The correct pairing is a tight envelope plus a mechanical ventilation system with dehumidification, which is standard in ACCA Manual RS ventilation guidance.

Are the same equipment brands used in Zone 2A as in dry climates?

The same manufacturers ship into Zone 2A, but the model selection within each brand shifts toward the variable-speed and high-latent-capacity lines. Standard single-stage models designed for dry-climate applications are often not the best fit even from the same manufacturer. The Manual S selection process picks the right model within the brand rather than picking the brand itself.

Do heat pumps make sense in Climate Zone 2A?

Heat pumps are increasingly common in Zone 2A because heating loads are modest and can be satisfied by the same equipment used for cooling. A cold-climate heat pump is not required in this zone; standard-performance heat pumps handle the small winter heating loads efficiently. The primary design question is still cooling and dehumidification, which drives equipment selection more than the heating side.

item.title: Oversized vs Undersized AC: What Sizing Errors Cost
item.description:
By the Editorial Team | Published: August 2026 | Last Updated: August 2026

The Real Cost of Getting the Tonnage Wrong

Sizing errors on residential cooling systems fall into two categories: oversizing, which is the vastly more common outcome of skipping the load calculation, and undersizing, which is rarer but more visible on the hottest days of the year. Both errors carry direct costs, both change the effective service life of the equipment, and both usually cost more to fix later than a correct load calculation would have cost up front. The dollar figures below draw on Building America and ENERGY STAR field studies of installed residential systems, plus utility bill impact estimates published by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory.

The two failure modes look different from the outside, but their causes trace to the same root: sizing to the wrong input. Oversizing usually comes from rules of thumb or from matching the outgoing system tonnage. Undersizing usually comes from bad envelope inputs or from cost-driven downsizing after the load calculation was done. Neither is the calculation fault.

The Oversizing Penalty

An oversized cooling system is one whose sensible capacity at design conditions exceeds the ACCA Manual S cap of 115 percent of the sensible load (or 125 percent for a heat pump). The equipment satisfies the thermostat quickly, shuts off, and does not run long enough to remove moisture from the air. The measurable outcomes are higher indoor humidity, higher electricity bills, more frequent compressor cycling, and shorter equipment life.

The most-cited field data on oversizing:

  • A typical oversized residential AC in a hot-humid climate cycles on and off 5 to 8 times per hour on mild days, versus 2 to 3 cycles per hour for a correctly sized unit.
  • Indoor relative humidity in oversized installations regularly runs 55 to 65 percent during the cooling season, compared with 45 to 55 percent for correctly sized systems.
  • Compressor service life shortens by an estimated 15 to 30 percent under high cycling counts, according to manufacturer service data.
  • Energy consumption per season runs 10 to 25 percent higher for oversized systems in cooling-dominant climates, driven by inrush current on each compressor startup.

The Hidden Cost: Retrofit Dehumidification

Homeowners who cannot tolerate the humidity from an oversized system typically add a whole-house dehumidifier, which costs $2,500 to $4,500 installed for a ducted unit in the 90-to-130 pint per day range. That expense is on top of the original oversized equipment. The correct equipment selection would have avoided both costs.

The Undersizing Penalty

An undersized system cannot reach setpoint on design days. The compressor runs continuously and still fails to lower the indoor temperature to the thermostat target during the hottest afternoon hours. The measurable outcomes are lost comfort during peak conditions, higher electricity bills from continuous operation, and, in the worst cases, refrigerant-side stress on the compressor.

Undersizing is much less common than oversizing in the U.S. residential market. The recurring root causes when it does happen:

  • Envelope inputs entered too favorably (understated solar heat gain, understated infiltration, over-assumed insulation values).
  • Designer trimming the calculated tonnage after the fact to fit a physical space constraint or hit a lower price point.
  • Recent additions or interior remodels that added conditioned floor area without triggering a fresh Manual J.
  • Ductwork downgrades (undersized returns, disconnected runs) that starve the equipment of airflow and drop delivered capacity.

Either way, the fix is equipment replacement or major duct rework, which is the most expensive corrective action on the list.

A Side-by-Side Cost Comparison

Sizing outcome Comfort effect Energy penalty (typical) Downstream cost to fix
Correctly sized (100 to 115 percent of load) Even temperatures; 45 to 55 percent RH Baseline None
Mildly oversized (116 to 130 percent of load) 50 to 60 percent RH; slight cycling +8 to +12 percent Tolerable without retrofit
Heavily oversized (140 percent and up) 60 percent and up RH; noticeable clamminess +15 to +25 percent Whole-house dehumidifier ($2,500 to $4,500)
Undersized (below load) Cannot reach setpoint on design days +10 to +20 percent (continuous run) Equipment replacement ($6,000 to $15,000)

Why Oversizing Is So Much More Common

Field studies consistently find that between 60 and 70 percent of installed residential cooling systems in the U.S. are oversized relative to a proper Manual J and Manual S selection. The reason is procedural: rules of thumb inflate the load, matching outgoing tonnage perpetuates prior oversizing, and contractors carry a slight bias toward one size up as a hedge against callbacks on the first hot day. The bias is understandable and the outcome is a systematic overspend and undercomfort across the market.

Is a slightly oversized system always a problem?

A system within the ACCA Manual S cap (up to 115 percent of sensible load for cooling, 125 percent for heat pumps in cooling mode) is not oversized by the standard definition. The design headroom exists to handle atypical peak days. Systems that exceed the cap start showing the humidity and cycling penalties in the first cooling season, and the severity scales with how far above the cap the selection sits. A 130 percent installation performs measurably worse than a 118 percent one.

Can a variable-speed system get away with being oversized?

A variable-speed unit can modulate down to roughly 25 percent of nameplate capacity, which lets it run long low-capacity cycles even when the nominal tonnage exceeds the load. In practice, this reduces the humidity penalty of oversizing but does not eliminate it, and the higher first cost of the oversized variable-speed unit is not recovered elsewhere. The Manual S cap still applies, and the guidance is to size a variable-speed unit near the load, not above it.

How can a homeowner tell if their existing system is oversized?

Three indicators reliably point to oversizing: short cycle times (compressor runs of under 10 minutes on mild days), indoor humidity readings above 55 percent during the cooling season, and cool but clammy air that leaves the thermostat satisfied while the house does not feel comfortable. A digital thermostat that logs runtime and a $15 hygrometer are enough to confirm the pattern.

What is the payback on right-sizing during equipment replacement?

Right-sizing at replacement typically costs the same or slightly less than replacing with the outgoing tonnage, because the correctly sized unit is often smaller. The savings show up in the utility bill and the humidity-complaint avoidance rather than a discrete payback figure. The stronger case is that failing to right-size costs money in both first cost (larger unit) and operating cost (higher energy use) simultaneously.

Does undersizing damage the compressor?

Continuous operation is within the compressor design envelope; the compressor itself does not fail from running long cycles. What does happen with undersized systems in humid climates is elevated refrigerant-side pressures if airflow is insufficient, which can shorten compressor life over years. The more common failure mode with undersizing is the homeowner replacing the entire system after a summer of poor comfort, not compressor failure.

If the old system was oversized, is a smaller replacement really safe?

A Manual J on the current envelope tells the whole story. If the calculation supports a smaller nominal tonnage, the smaller unit will cool the house at design conditions with 15 percent headroom (per Manual S). The instinct to match what was there is the mechanism that perpetuates oversizing across equipment generations, and a well-documented load calculation is the objective evidence needed to break out of that cycle.

Do utility rebate programs check for sizing compliance?

Utility rebate programs for high-efficiency equipment increasingly require documentation of Manual J and Manual S as a condition of the rebate, following ACCA Quality Installation and ENERGY STAR Home Upgrade guidelines. The rebate documentation requirement is one of the more effective enforcement mechanisms for load calculations in the U.S. residential market, because it ties a cash incentive to the calculation being performed.

How much of the oversizing problem is fixable at commissioning?

Very little. Sensible capacity and sensible heat ratio are equipment characteristics, not commissioning settings. Airflow can be tuned down modestly to shift capacity toward latent, and thermostat setback strategies can smooth cycling, but neither addresses the underlying capacity mismatch. Fixing sizing after installation requires equipment replacement, which is why the load calculation before purchase carries so much leverage.

  • Energy consumption per season runs 10 to 25 percent higher for oversized systems in cooling-dominant climates, driven by inrush current on each compressor startup.

The Hidden Cost: Retrofit Dehumidification

Homeowners who cannot tolerate the humidity from an oversized system typically add a whole-house dehumidifier, which costs $2,500 to $4,500 installed for a ducted unit in the 90-to-130 pint per day range. That expense is on top of the original oversized equipment. The correct equipment selection would have avoided both costs.

The Undersizing Penalty

An undersized system cannot reach setpoint on design days. The compressor runs continuously and still fails to lower the indoor temperature to the thermostat target during the hottest afternoon hours. The measurable outcomes are lost comfort during peak conditions, higher electricity bills from continuous operation, and, in the worst cases, refrigerant-side stress on the compressor.

Undersizing is much less common than oversizing in the U.S. residential market. The recurring root causes when it does happen:

  • Envelope inputs entered too favorably (understated solar heat gain, understated infiltration, over-assumed insulation values).
  • Designer trimming the calculated tonnage after the fact to fit a physical space constraint or hit a lower price point.
  • Recent additions or interior remodels that added conditioned floor area without triggering a fresh Manual J.
  • Ductwork downgrades (undersized returns, disconnected runs) that starve the equipment of airflow and drop delivered capacity.

Either way, the fix is equipment replacement or major duct rework, which is the most expensive corrective action on the list.

A Side-by-Side Cost Comparison

Mildly oversized (116 to 130 percent of load) 50 to 60 percent RH; slight cycling +8 to +12 percent Tolerable without retrofit
Heavily oversized (140 percent and up) 60 percent and up RH; noticeable clamminess +15 to +25 percent Whole-house dehumidifier ($2,500 to $4,500)

Why Oversizing Is So Much More Common

Field studies consistently find that between 60 and 70 percent of installed residential cooling systems in the U.S. are oversized relative to a proper Manual J and Manual S selection. The reason is procedural: rules of thumb inflate the load, matching outgoing tonnage perpetuates prior oversizing, and contractors carry a slight bias toward one size up as a hedge against callbacks on the first hot day. The bias is understandable and the outcome is a systematic overspend and undercomfort across the market.

Is a slightly oversized system always a problem?

A system within the ACCA Manual S cap (up to 115 percent of sensible load for cooling, 125 percent for heat pumps in cooling mode) is not oversized by the standard definition. The design headroom exists to handle atypical peak days. Systems that exceed the cap start showing the humidity and cycling penalties in the first cooling season, and the severity scales with how far above the cap the selection sits. A 130 percent installation performs measurably worse than a 118 percent one.

Can a variable-speed system get away with being oversized?

A variable-speed unit can modulate down to roughly 25 percent of nameplate capacity, which lets it run long low-capacity cycles even when the nominal tonnage exceeds the load. In practice, this reduces the humidity penalty of oversizing but does not eliminate it, and the higher first cost of the oversized variable-speed unit is not recovered elsewhere. The Manual S cap still applies, and the guidance is to size a variable-speed unit near the load, not above it.

How can a homeowner tell if their existing system is oversized?

Three indicators reliably point to oversizing: short cycle times (compressor runs of under 10 minutes on mild days), indoor humidity readings above 55 percent during the cooling season, and cool but clammy air that leaves the thermostat satisfied while the house does not feel comfortable. A digital thermostat that logs runtime and a $15 hygrometer are enough to confirm the pattern.

Right-sizing at replacement typically costs the same or slightly less than replacing with the outgoing tonnage, because the correctly sized unit is often smaller. The savings show up in the utility bill and the humidity-complaint avoidance rather than a discrete payback figure. The stronger case is that failing to right-size costs money in both first cost (larger unit) and operating cost (higher energy use) simultaneously.

Does undersizing damage the compressor?

Continuous operation is within the compressor design envelope; the compressor itself does not fail from running long cycles. What does happen with undersized systems in humid climates is elevated refrigerant-side pressures if airflow is insufficient, which can shorten compressor life over years. The more common failure mode with undersizing is the homeowner replacing the entire system after a summer of poor comfort, not compressor failure.

If the old system was oversized, is a smaller replacement really safe?

A Manual J on the current envelope tells the whole story. If the calculation supports a smaller nominal tonnage, the smaller unit will cool the house at design conditions with 15 percent headroom (per Manual S). The instinct to match what was there is the mechanism that perpetuates oversizing across equipment generations, and a well-documented load calculation is the objective evidence needed to break out of that cycle.

Utility rebate programs for high-efficiency equipment increasingly require documentation of Manual J and Manual S as a condition of the rebate, following ACCA Quality Installation and ENERGY STAR Home Upgrade guidelines. The rebate documentation requirement is one of the more effective enforcement mechanisms for load calculations in the U.S. residential market, because it ties a cash incentive to the calculation being performed.

Very little. Sensible capacity and sensible heat ratio are equipment characteristics, not commissioning settings. Airflow can be tuned down modestly to shift capacity toward latent, and thermostat setback strategies can smooth cycling, but neither addresses the underlying capacity mismatch. Fixing sizing after installation requires equipment replacement, which is why the load calculation before purchase carries so much leverage.

By the Editorial Team | Published: August 2026 | Last Updated: August 2026

Why Duct Design Belongs in the Same Conversation as Load Calculation

Duct design is the third of the three ACCA manuals that anchor residential cooling design. Manual J produces the loads. Manual S selects equipment sized to those loads. Manual D sizes the duct system that actually delivers the equipment capacity to the rooms that need it. Skipping Manual D is a common cause of installations where the right equipment was picked but rooms still miss setpoint, because the airflow arrives unevenly or the blower fights static pressure it was not rated for.

The Manual D procedure takes the per-room loads from the Manual J run, converts them to per-room cubic feet per minute of required airflow, and then sizes trunks, branches, and diffusers so that airflow arrives at each room within the equipment rated external static pressure. It is a design activity, not a rule of thumb. Rules like eight-inch trunk with six-inch branches produce duct systems that occasionally work by luck and frequently do not.

The Airflow Conversion

Airflow requirement per room is derived from the room sensible load and the temperature difference between the supply air and the room air. The standard formula is CFM equals sensible Btu per hour divided by (1.08 times the design temperature rise), where 1.08 is the standard air constant at typical conditions. A room with a 4,320 Btu/hr sensible load and a 20-degree design rise needs 200 CFM of conditioned air.

Once each room CFM requirement is set, the trunk carries the sum of all downstream branch requirements. Every fitting, elbow, boot, and diffuser adds pressure loss, expressed in equivalent length of straight duct. Manual D tallies those equivalent lengths across the design longest and shortest paths, checks that the friction rate lands in the target range (typically 0.08 to 0.10 inches of water column per 100 feet), and adjusts sizes accordingly.

External Static Pressure and Why It Governs Everything

Every air handler and furnace is rated for a maximum external static pressure, typically 0.5 inches of water column for residential equipment. That number is the total pressure the blower can overcome across the entire duct system, from the return grille to the supply diffuser. If the installed duct system exceeds 0.5 inches, the blower cannot deliver its rated airflow, and every downstream calculation (including the Manual S equipment selection) becomes invalid.

The static pressure budget divides across the components:

  • Return path (grille, filter, return trunk): typically 0.15 to 0.20 inches of water column.
  • Coil and cabinet: 0.15 to 0.25 inches, taken from manufacturer data at design airflow.
  • Supply trunk, branches, and diffusers: whatever remains from the 0.5-inch budget, typically 0.10 to 0.20 inches.

The single most common cause of over-static installations is an undersized return path. A one-inch pleated filter in a small return grille can pull 0.25 inches by itself, which leaves almost no budget for the supply side and forces the blower into deratable operation. Manual D catches this on paper before the ductboard gets cut.

Friction Rate and Duct Sizing

Friction rate is the design target for how much static pressure the duct system is allowed to lose per 100 feet of equivalent length. The rate is calculated by dividing the available static (after coil, cabinet, and return budget) by the total equivalent length of the longest supply run, then multiplying by 100. A typical residential system lands at 0.08 to 0.10 inches per 100 feet.

Once the friction rate is set, duct sizes are read from an ACCA ductulator or the ductwork sizing table in Manual D. Higher friction rates permit smaller ducts (more restrictive), lower friction rates require larger ducts. The trade-off is between duct cost and blower energy: undersized ducts save material but increase fan energy use and noise, while oversized ducts cost more but run quieter and give the blower headroom.

Duct Leakage and Its Effect on Delivered Capacity

Ductwork leakage is measured in cubic feet per minute at a reference pressure (25 pascals for total leakage, or CFM25). The 2021 IECC caps total duct leakage at 4 CFM25 per 100 square feet of conditioned floor area when the ducts are in unconditioned space. Systems built without leakage testing frequently exceed twice that number.

Duct leakage translates directly into lost capacity, and in unconditioned attics it also imports moisture through return leakage on the suction side. The Manual D design assumes a leakage rate; if the installed system leaks more, the delivered capacity drops, room airflows underperform, and the equipment appears undersized even though the load calculation and selection were correct.

The high-leverage sealing points on a residential duct system, ranked by typical contribution to total leakage:

  • Boot-to-drywall connections at every supply register and return grille.
  • Trunk-to-plenum joints, especially at the air handler cabinet.
  • Branch takeoffs where flex duct connects to metal trunks.
  • Return-side platform returns and stud-cavity returns (avoid entirely when possible).
  • Filter rack seams and access-panel gaskets on the air handler.

Friction Rate Ranges by System Type

System type Typical friction rate (in. w.c. per 100 ft) Notes
Standard residential, sheet metal 0.08 to 0.10 Baseline; used in most single-family design
Flex duct branches 0.05 to 0.08 Lower; flex has higher inherent friction, size up
High-static equipment (ECM blowers) 0.10 to 0.12 Slightly higher permitted; still watch static budget
Retrofit into existing plenum 0.05 to 0.08 Constrained; may require duct redesign, not just resizing

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Manual D required if Manual J and Manual S are done?

Manual D is referenced by the International Residential Code alongside Manual J and Manual S as the accepted procedure for duct design. Skipping it while doing J and S produces a system with correct equipment tonnage and incorrect airflow distribution, which is one of the most common patterns in the AC works but this room is always warm complaints. All three manuals are required to produce a design that performs as calculated.

Can flex duct be used throughout or should trunks be sheet metal?

Flex duct is acceptable for branch runs when installed straight, supported at manufacturer-recommended intervals, and sized for its higher inherent friction (typically one duct size larger than the equivalent metal branch). Long trunk runs in flex are difficult to install without sag and bend penalties that inflate the friction rate. Best practice on modern residential design is metal trunks with flex branches, sized per Manual D, not by convention.

What is the practical difference between a Manual D design and a rule-of-thumb duct layout?

A Manual D design starts from per-room loads and produces a duct layout that delivers the required airflow to each room within a specified friction rate. A rule-of-thumb layout uses standard sizes (an eight-inch trunk with six-inch branches, for example) regardless of load or run length. The results diverge sharply in houses with long branches, multiple stories, or asymmetric room loads, which is most modern residential construction.

How is static pressure measured after installation?

External static pressure is measured with a manometer (analog or digital) reading pressure differences across the air handler. The technician drills small test ports on the supply and return sides of the coil and cabinet, records the readings during equipment operation, and compares the total against the manufacturer rated maximum. Static above rated is a red flag for a duct system that cannot deliver design airflow. TrueFlow plates and similar tools also measure airflow directly at the air handler.

Why do so many installed systems have static-pressure problems?

Installed systems trend toward over-static because return sides are frequently under-designed. A single return grille sized for aesthetics or drywall convenience rarely provides the throat area needed for the required CFM. Filter racks add pressure that is invisible until measured. Manual D flags both issues at design time, but only if it is actually run.

Does an ECM blower solve a static-pressure problem?

Electronically commutated motor (ECM) blowers can compensate for higher static than a permanent split capacitor (PSC) blower, holding rated airflow up to a higher pressure ceiling. That masks the underlying duct problem rather than solving it: the blower runs at higher watts, noise increases, and delivered capacity still drops if the duct system leaks or has poor branch balance. The correct fix is a properly designed duct system with the ECM blower operating well within its curve.

How does duct leakage testing work?

Duct leakage testing seals every register and return with removable tape or plates, connects a calibrated fan to the duct system through the air handler cabinet, and pressurizes the system to a reference pressure (typically 25 pascals). The fan calibrated airflow at that pressure equals the total leakage rate in CFM25. The 2021 IECC and most state adoptions require this test on all new-construction residential systems and set the pass threshold at 4 CFM25 per 100 square feet.

Should ducts always be brought into conditioned space?

Ducts in conditioned space perform measurably better than ducts in unconditioned attics or crawls, because they avoid both conduction losses to the extreme ambient and moisture penalties from leakage. On new construction, sealed attics or drop soffits routinely bring the duct system into conditioned space at modest incremental cost. On retrofits, the change is more expensive and often only makes financial sense during a major remodel. When ducts stay in an unconditioned attic, tight sealing and R-8 insulation are the minimum interventions.
